blocks.heading: Choosing a production method
blocks.text: Choose by demand volume, required variety, available skills and equipment, reliability, cost and quality. Job production fits individual specifications, batch can fit recurring groups with variety and flow can fit large dependable standard demand. The cheapest-looking method is unsuitable if it cannot meet customers’ needs or its capacity sits idle. Job production is not on-the-job training: one makes an output and the other develops a worker. On-the-job and off-the-job learning are methods explained in topic 3.5.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Joinery receives different custom dimensions for each order and has skilled flexible workers but no large standard contract. Job production fits the variety and skill. A flow line could restrict customisation and commit funds before standard demand exists. Prefer job production here and review if large repeat orders emerge.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why Nela Joinery making one custom cabinet is different from an experienced worker teaching a new worker at the bench.

Making the one-off cabinet describes job production. Teaching while working is on-the-job training, a method of skill development. Off-the-job training is the alternative learning setting. Production method and learning method answer different questions.
